sections.heading: How to turn a picture into an Excel sheet
sections.body:
Use a clear picture of one table. The tool reads the rows and columns, then gives you the table as text that Excel can open. You do not install anything, and you do not need an account.

1. Open [Image to Excel](https://image-to-excel.lazur.app/).
2. Choose the picture from your computer. It can be a JPG, a PNG or another image file up to 15 MB.
3. Wait while the AI reads it. The answer usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds.
4. Click copy to take the whole result in one click.
5. Paste it into a plain text file, save the file as table.csv, and open it in Excel.

The result is only the table. There is no intro sentence and no code fence, so everything you copy is data.

sections.heading: What the CSV looks like
sections.body:
A CSV is plain text. Each line is one row, and each comma starts a new column. The first row is the header, so it works as the column names. If a value contains a comma or a quote, the tool wraps that value in double quotes, so a cell such as 1,250 stays in one cell and does not split into two.

**Open the file, do not paste the text straight in.** Plain text pasted into Excel can land in a single column. Saving it as a .csv file and opening that file lets Excel split each value into its own cell.

sections.heading: Check the numbers against the picture
sections.body:
An AI reads the picture, so check the result before you use it. Look hardest at numbers that look alike, such as 3 and 8, 1 and 7, or 0 and 6. Check decimal points and dates too. Compare the first and last rows with the picture, then add up one column yourself and compare the total.

Blur, glare and a tilted camera make digits harder to read, so fix those first. Shoot straight on, in good light, with the whole table in focus. Crop out anything that is not part of the table. A clean screenshot works too.

sections.heading: Free runs and the email step
sections.body:
You get 3 free runs a day. When you have used them, leave an email to get 3 more. No account and no password are needed to start.

To make the most of your runs, put the whole table in one picture and run it once. A single clear picture of a full table uses one run. Several small pictures use several runs.

sections.heading: Excel can read a picture too
sections.body:
Microsoft 365 has its own option. On Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 1903 or later, select **Data > From Picture** in Excel, choose Picture From File or Picture From Clipboard, check the result, and select Insert Data. It also needs the Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime. [Microsoft's guide](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/insert-data-from-picture) has the Mac, web and phone steps.

Use Excel's option if you already work in Microsoft 365 and want the table placed straight into a sheet. Use this tool if you want a CSV file or do not have that version of Excel.

If you dictate notes into Excel or other apps every day, Lazur does this in any app on your Mac. Hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

sections.heading: Convert an image to Excel online, step by step

This is an AI converter. Your picture goes to Google Gemini on Lazur's servers, which reads the table and sends back CSV text. You use it in the browser, with nothing to install.

If you paste the text straight into a sheet, the rows can stack in one column. Opening the .csv file avoids that, because Excel splits each value at its comma.

sections.heading: What to put in the picture
sections.body:
Printed tables give the cleanest result. Take the picture so the whole table is in the frame and in focus. Keep the header row in the picture, because the tool uses the first row as the header in the CSV. Leave out notes, logos and other text that sits outside the table, so they do not end up in your data.

Keep the file under 15 MB. A phone photo at normal settings is usually well under that. If the picture is handwritten, read every value against the original before you use it, since handwriting is harder for any reader to get right.

sections.heading: From the CSV to a working Excel sheet
sections.body:
A CSV file has one line per row, and commas separate the values. The tool wraps any value that has a comma or a quote in double quotes, so that value stays in one cell.

**Save the copied text as table.csv before you open it.** The file name ending in .csv tells Excel to split the values into columns. Once the file opens, check that the column names in the first row match the picture, then save the file as an Excel workbook if you want to keep formatting.

sections.heading: Free runs: 3 a day, then 3 more with an email
sections.body:
You get 3 free runs a day. After those, leave an email to get 3 more runs. You do not need an account to start, and you do not need to log in.

Each run is one picture. If a table runs across two pictures, you will use two runs. Taking one clear picture of the full table saves runs and keeps the rows in one piece.

sections.heading: Check the result before you use it
sections.body:
The AI reads the picture, so check the numbers against it. Look most closely at digits that are easy to mix up, such as 3 and 8, 1 and 7, and 0 and 6. Check decimal points, and check dates in the format the picture uses.

A quick test is to add up one column and compare the total with the total in the picture. If the sums match, the column is probably right. If they do not match, look at the values in that column first, then run the picture again with a sharper photo.

sections.heading: What OCR does with a table
sections.body:
OCR, or optical character recognition, turns the letters and numbers in an image into text you can edit. With a table, the reader also has to keep the rows and columns in order, so each value lands in the right cell.

This tool sends your picture to Google Gemini on Lazur's servers and asks for the table as CSV. Plain text with commas is enough for Excel to rebuild the grid once you open it as a .csv file.

sections.heading: Get a table from an image with OCR
sections.body:
1. Open the [OCR table tool](https://image-to-excel.lazur.app/ocr).
2. Upload a JPG, PNG or another image file up to 15 MB.
3. Wait about 1 to 3 seconds for the table to come back.
4. Click copy, paste the text into a plain text file, and save it as table.csv.
5. Open table.csv in Excel and check the values against the picture.

A scan works well when it is clear and flat. Scan the page at a good resolution, keep the whole table inside the edges, and avoid shadows across the rows.

sections.heading: Excel's own option for pictures
sections.body:
Microsoft 365 can read a table from a picture without a separate tool. On Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 1903 or later, go to **Data > From Picture** and choose Picture From File or Picture From Clipboard. Wait while the Data from Picture dialog analyzes the image, check the results, and select Insert Data. The Windows version also needs the Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime.

On a Mac, the steps are Data > Data From Picture, then Picture From File or Picture From Clipboard, and Insert Data at the end. The web and phone steps are on [Microsoft's guide](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/insert-data-from-picture).

sections.heading: Which one to use
sections.body:
Use Excel's option if you already have Microsoft 365 and want the table placed straight into a sheet after you review it. It works best with the character sets Microsoft lists, and it asks you to shoot head-on with the data in focus.

Use this tool if you want a CSV file, do not have that version of Excel, or want to convert a picture on a computer where you do not use Excel's From Picture option. The tool takes images up to 15 MB and gives you 3 free runs a day, with 3 more after you leave an email.

sections.heading: Check OCR results for common misreads
sections.body:
OCR errors follow patterns. Letter O and number 0 look alike, and so do letter l, the number 1 and the letter I. Letter S can read as 5, and B as 8. Check those first in names, codes and totals.

Decimal points and thousands separators also cause trouble. 1.250,00 and 1,250.00 are different amounts, so look at the picture to see which style the table uses. Then add up a column and compare the total with the picture.

faq.q: Can I use OCR in Excel?
faq.a: Yes. In Microsoft 365, select Data, then Data From Picture, and choose a picture file or a clipboard screenshot. On Windows you need Windows 11 or Windows 10 version 1903 or later, plus the WebView2 Runtime. Review the result before you select Insert Data.

faq.q: How do I convert a JPG image to Excel using OCR?
faq.a: Upload the JPG to this tool, wait a few seconds, and click copy. Paste the text into a plain text file and save it as table.csv. Open that file in Excel, and the first row becomes the header. Check the numbers against the picture before you use them.

faq.q: Can Excel pull data from an image?
faq.a: Yes, with Data From Picture in Microsoft 365. Excel reads a table from a picture file or a clipboard screenshot and shows the result for review. You then choose Insert Data to place it in the sheet. Microsoft's guide lists the steps for each platform.
